days.title: Arrays & Hashing + Prefix-Sum Counting
days.intro: Today is about one big idea: trade space for time with a hash map or hash set. Almost every brute force here is "for each element, scan the rest" (O(n²)); the optimal version asks "what do I need to have seen already to answer this in O(1)?" and stores exactly that in a map. The second idea is prefix sums (and prefix XORs): a subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums, so "count subarrays with sum K" becomes "count earlier prefixes equal to prefix - K ". Most questions are warm-ups, so move fast on them. Spend your real time on Longest Consecutive Sequence, Count Inversions / Reverse Pairs (merge-sort counting) and the subarray-sum family. For every problem, practise saying the brute force and its complexity out loud first, then improve it step by step.

days.title: Two Pointers + Sliding Window
days.intro: Today is about walking through an array with two indices instead of two nested loops. Two pointers works when the array is sorted (or can be sorted) or when you are comparing the two ends: each step you throw away one candidate for good, so the whole scan is O(n). Sliding window is two pointers moving in the same direction over a contiguous range. Learn one variable-window template and reuse it everywhere: expand right one step, update your counts, then shrink left while the window is invalid, and record the answer when it is valid. For "count subarrays with exactly K" problems, remember the trick exactly(K) = atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1) .

days.title: Stacks + Monotonic Stack
days.intro: Today is stack day, and most of it is one idea: the monotonic stack. Whenever a problem asks "for each element, find the nearest element to the left/right that is bigger/smaller", you can answer it for all elements in one O(n) pass by keeping a stack whose values stay sorted. Each element is pushed once and popped once, which is why the pass is linear even though there is a loop inside a loop. Next Greater Element is the template; Daily Temperatures, Stock Span, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Sum of Subarray Minimums and Remove K Digits are all the same idea with a different question asked at pop time. For each problem ask yourself three things: (1) what do I store on the stack (index or value), (2) should the stack be increasing or decreasing, (3) what do I compute when I pop. The other problems today (parentheses, RPN, asteroids, Min Stack, LFU Cache) use a stack or a clever data structure to remember "the most recent unfinished thing".

days.title: Binary Search + Binary Search on Answer
days.intro: Binary search comes in two flavours. Search on an index: the array is sorted (or sorted in pieces, like a rotated array), and each comparison throws away half of the indices. Search on the answer: the array is not what you search at all; you search a range of possible answers (an eating speed, a distance, a page limit) and ask a yes/no question "is this answer feasible?" whose result flips exactly once (false false false true true true). For both, use one template and stick to it: lo , hi , while (lo <= hi) , mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 , and keep a variable ans that you update whenever mid is a valid candidate. Before coding, always say out loud what is monotonic, because that is the whole reason binary search works.

days.title: Linked Lists
days.intro: Master three moves first: reverse, fast/slow pointers, and the dummy head. Nearly every linked list problem is a combination of these. Reversal is three pointers ( prev , curr , next ) and must become muscle memory. Fast/slow pointers find the middle, detect cycles, find the cycle start and give "k-th from the end" in one pass. A dummy node in front of the head removes every "what if the head itself changes?" special case. Before you code, draw 4 boxes on paper and move the arrows by hand; most linked list bugs are lost references, and drawing catches them. Always ask yourself: "what happens with an empty list, one node, and two nodes?"

days.title: Binary Trees (DFS) + Level-Order BFS
days.intro: Today is mostly ONE recursion pattern: "ask my left child, ask my right child, combine the two answers, return something to my parent". Height, diameter, balance, max path sum and good nodes are all that pattern; the only question each time is what do I return upward and what global answer do I update on the way. The second pattern is BFS with a queue, processed one level at a time ( size = queue.size() before the inner loop) — level order, right/left view and max width all use it. For BST questions, always ask "how does the ordering (left < node < right) let me skip half the tree, or give me sorted order via inorder?". Before coding any tree question, say out loud: base case (null), what the recursion returns, and the complexity O(n) time / O(h) stack space, where h is O(log n) for a balanced tree and O(n) for a skewed one.

days.title: Binary Trees (Part 2) + Binary Search Trees
days.intro: Today has three families of problems. (1) Views and orderings (top view, vertical order, boundary): give every node a coordinate (row = depth, column = horizontal distance) and decide which node "wins" each coordinate; BFS is your friend because it meets nodes top-to-bottom, left- to-right. (2) "Treat the tree as a graph" (nodes at distance K, burn the tree): a tree node only knows its children, so first build a parent map, then run a plain BFS outward from the start node. (3) BST operations (insert, delete, successor, construct, two sum, recover, largest BST): always ask "how does the BST ordering let me throw away half the tree?" and "what does inorder (sorted order) tell me?". Most BST answers are O(h) walks or one inorder pass. Morris traversal is a nice-to- know O(1)-space trick; if you are short on time, learn it during revision.

days.title: Heaps + Tries
days.intro: Today has two tools. A heap answers "what is the smallest (or largest) item right now?" in O(1) and lets you add or remove in O(log n). Reach for it whenever you see top K, K-th largest, closest K, merge many sorted streams, or median of a stream. The trick for top-K is counter-intuitive: to keep the K largest, keep a min-heap of size K, so the weakest of the winners sits on top and is easy to throw out. Also learn how a heap works inside (array, parent = (i-1)/2 , children 2i+1 and 2i+2 , sift up, sift down), because Striver's three heap questions ask you to build one by hand. A trie is a tree of characters: every path from the root spells a prefix, so prefix questions cost O(length of word) no matter how many words are stored. Implement the plain trie until you can write it in two minutes, then every trie question is "plain trie + one extra field per node" (a counter, a stored word, an end flag). The two XOR problems use a bitwise trie (each node has children 0 and 1); do them last. Java has PriorityQueue ; JavaScript has no built-in heap, so the JS solutions carry a small Heap class. Write it once from memory, it is the same 30 lines every time.

days.title: Recursion & Backtracking + Math & Geometry
days.intro: Backtracking is one template: choose, recurse, un-choose. Every problem today in the first section is a walk over a decision tree: at each node you pick an option, go deeper, then undo the pick so the next option starts from a clean state. Before you code anything else, draw the recursion tree for Subsets on paper (include/exclude each element) and you will see that Combination Sum, Permutations, Palindrome Partitioning and N-Queens are the same tree with different branching rules and different pruning. Ask yourself three questions for every problem: (1) what is one "choice"? (2) when is a path complete? (3) what can I prune early? Duplicates are always handled the same way: sort first, then skip equal values at the same tree level. The math and matrix problems in the second section are quick breathers: they reward careful index handling (layers, boundaries, in-place markers) rather than clever algorithms.

days.title: Graphs: Traversal + Connectivity
days.intro: Today is the longest day, but most of it is one idea repeated: visit every node once, and remember what you visited. A grid is just a graph where each cell has 4 (or 8) neighbours, so Number of Islands, Max Area, Flood Fill, Surrounded Regions and Pacific Atlantic are all the same DFS/BFS with a different rule for "can I step here?". Use multi-source BFS when the question asks for the shortest distance or time from the nearest of many sources (Rotting Oranges, Walls and Gates, Nearest 1). Use topological sort (Kahn's in-degree BFS, or DFS finish order) whenever there are dependencies or you must detect a cycle in a directed graph. Use Union-Find when edges arrive one at a time and you ask "are these already connected?". Get Number of Islands and Kahn's algorithm solid first. Bridges, Articulation Points and Kosaraju are the hardest: they all rely on DFS discovery times, so learn them as one family at the end. GRAPHS: TRAVERSAL & CONNECTIVITY 10.1 Clone Graph Medium 519 10.2 Course Schedule Medium 522 10.3 Course Schedule II Medium 525 10.4 Graph Valid Tree Medium 528 10.5 Max Area of Island Medium 531 10.6 Number of Connected Components In An Undirected Graph Medium 534 10.7 Number of Islands Medium 538 10.8 Pacific Atlantic Water Flow Medium 541 10.9 Redundant Connection Medium 545 10.10 Rotting Oranges Medium 548 10.11 Surrounded Regions Medium 551

days.title: Shortest Paths + Disjoint Set & MST
days.intro: Today is about two families of graph tools. First, shortest paths: pick the algorithm from the edge weights. All weights equal means plain BFS. A DAG means topological order plus relaxation. Non- negative weights means Dijkstra with a min-heap. Negative weights, or a cap on the number of edges, means Bellman-Ford. All pairs on a small graph means Floyd-Warshall. Many grid problems ("minimise the maximum height on a path") are Dijkstra in disguise where the path cost is a max instead of a sum. Second, the Disjoint Set Union (DSU): learn find with path compression and union by rank/size until you can write it in two minutes, then reuse it for Kruskal's MST, counting components, and dynamic island problems. Before coding any problem today, say out loud: "What are the nodes, what are the edges, what is the weight, and what does the path cost combine with (sum or max)?" GRAPHS: PATHS & SPANNING TREES 11.1 Network Delay Time Medium 601 11.2 Reconstruct Itinerary Hard 605 11.3 Min Cost to Connect All Points Medium 608 11.4 Swim In Rising Water Hard 612 11.5 Alien Dictionary Hard 617 11.6 Cheapest Flights Within K Stops Medium 621 11.7 Shortest Path in Undirected Graph with Unit Weights Medium 624 11.8 Shortest Path in DAG Medium 627 11.9 Dijkstra's Algorithm Medium 630 11.10 Path With Minimum Effort Medium 633 11.11 Bellman-Ford Algorithm Medium 638

days.title: 1D DP + Knapsack & Grids
days.intro: Today is DP part 1. Almost every problem here follows one recipe: (1) define a state in words ("f(i) = best answer for the first i items"), (2) write the recursion that tries every choice at that state, (3) notice the same states are solved again and again, so cache them (memoization), (4) flip the recursion into a loop that fills a table from the base cases up (tabulation), and (5) notice each row only needs the previous row or two, so keep just those (space optimization). Interviewers love hearing you walk this ladder out loud. Don't jump straight to the table: the recursion is where you prove the state and transitions are right, and everything after it is mechanical. Watch for three families today: "last step came from i-1 or i-2" (stairs, robber, decode ways), "take it or leave it" knapsack (coin change, subset sum, target sum), and grid paths (unique paths, longest increasing path).

days.title: DP on Strings + Stocks, LIS & Partition DP
days.intro: Today is DP part 2. Almost every string problem here is a cousin of Longest Common Subsequence: define f(i, j) over a position in each string, ask "do the current characters match?", and branch. Stock problems are a small state machine (day, holding or not, transactions left), LIS problems build on "best answer ending at index i", and partition DP (Matrix Chain, Burst Balloons, Palindrome Partitioning II) tries every split point k inside an interval [i, j] . For each problem, follow the same ladder out loud: write the recursion, add a memo table, turn it into a bottom-up table, then shrink the table to one or two rows. Interviewers reward that progression more than a memorised final answer.

days.title: Greedy + Intervals
days.intro: Greedy problems reward one question: "what is the locally best move, and why can it never hurt me later?" Most of today's problems collapse to a single pass once you find the right quantity to track (best sum ending here, farthest reachable index, current fuel surplus, range of possible open brackets). Interval problems are even more mechanical: the whole trick is choosing the sort key. Sort by start when you want to merge or insert (Merge Intervals, Insert Interval, Meeting Rooms). Sort by end when you want to keep as many non-overlapping intervals as possible (Non- overlapping Intervals, N meetings in one room). When you need "how many overlap at once" (Meeting Rooms II, platforms), sort starts and ends separately and sweep. Don't burn interview time on formal proofs; give a one-line exchange argument ("swapping in the one that ends earlier never makes things worse") and move on.

days.title: Bit Manipulation + String Matching
days.intro: Last day: keep new material light and spend most of your time on revision. Bit manipulation rests on a handful of identities: x ^ x = 0 , x ^ 0 = x , n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, n & - n isolates it, and (n >> i) & 1 reads bit i. String matching is about not re-comparing characters you already know about: Rabin-Karp reuses a rolling hash, while Z-function and KMP reuse previously matched prefixes. Learn the LPS array well; it solves several "hard" string problems in O(n). After the morning, re-solve any must-do questions you skipped and redo 1–2 problems per pattern from memory, with a timer running.
